newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Bills close weaker as NZ dlr TWI continues easing.
newsitem.headline: Bills close weaker as NZ dlr TWI continues easing.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (JUN) 92.77 (PREV 92.88) 90-DAYS 7.18 (PREV 7.01)
OVERNIGHT CASH 6.70 PCT (PREV 6.50) US 5-YR 6.55 (PREV 6.50)
* NZ bank bills close sharply weaker on lower TWI
* Conditions still about 80 points easier than RBNZ desires * Trade in bond market subdued ahead of U.S. FOMC meeting

New Zealand bank bill rates closed sharply higher on Monday after the dollar's Trade- Weighted Index continued to fall, leaving monetary conditions considerably easier than the central bank's desired level.

Dealers in the money market said the prognosis for the short end of the yield curve was not good, with the 90-day bill rate still about 80 basis points below the Reserve Bank's desired policy setting in relation to the TWI.
"Obviously conditions are a little bit easy, so there's still a bit of pressure on the front end based on the Reserve Bank's view," said one dealer.
The 90-day bank bill rate spiked 17 points higher to close around 7.18 percent as the TWI continued to fall, ending at 67.32 from 67.73 at Friday's close.
In March the Reserve Bank indicated it preferred a 90-day rate of 7.5 percent and the TWI at 68.0, or an equivalent mix.

Last week, the Reserve Bank sought a firming of conditions when both the Kiwi dollar and 90-day rate eased too far below its desired mix. The Kiwi rallied on the comment, but weakness over the weekend on a TWI sent overall conditions easier again.
"There don't seem to be too many positive things out there for the bill market at the moment," said another dealer.
"It doesn't look too positive at all, actually."
He said 7.20 percent should provide some sort of intermediate support for the 90-days but if that didn't hold, 7.25 percent, even up towards 7.50 percent, was on the cards.
Bond yields rose around 10 points in sympathy with U.S. Treasury weakness and influenced by the soft short end tone.
But bond trade was subdued, dealers said, with most players content to wait for Tuesday's U.S. FOMC meeting, with many divided on whether the Fed would raise its federal funds rate.
"People, either way, would be pretty happy to see a rate hike (in the U.S.) and see higher yields so they could buy it -- I still think the market wants to be bought," one dealer said.
-- Matthew Brockett, Wellington Newsroom (64 4) 473-3736
